title: Delay the Resolution of Each Promise
statement:
Write `delayAll(functions, ms)`. Each entry of `functions` takes no arguments and gives back a promise when called. Return a new array of functions, one for each entry and in the same order. Calling the new function at index `i` runs `functions[i]` and gives back a promise that ends the same way as the promise of `functions[i]`, resolving with the same value or rejecting with the same reason, but `ms` milliseconds after that original promise settled.

Each case describes `functions` as JSON. An entry `{ t, resolve }` is a function whose promise resolves with the value `resolve` after `t` ms; `{ t, reject }` rejects with the string `reject` after `t` ms. When `t` is `0` the promise is already settled when the function returns. The judge calls `delayAll(functions, ms)` and then calls every function of the returned array at time `0`, in order. The answer has one entry per returned function, in the same order: `{ t, status: "fulfilled", value }` or `{ t, status: "rejected", reason }`, where `t` is when its promise settled, in ms from the start.
constraints: Each function is { t, resolve } or { t, reject }
resolve is an integer from -1000 to 1000
reject is a string of 1 to 20 characters
api: delayAll(functions: Array<() => Promise<any>>, ms: number): Array<() => Promise<any>>
notes:
## Intuition

Each new function is a thin wrapper around one original function. It calls the original, waits for its promise to settle, and then waits `ms` more before passing the very same outcome on. A wrapper can only decide when its promise settles if it creates that promise itself, so it returns `new Promise(...)` and keeps `resolve` and `reject`. Both outcomes need a handler, each of which starts a `setTimeout` for `ms`. The wrappers are independent, so when they all run at once each one is shifted by exactly `ms`; the delays do not add up. (The brute force does the same with `async`/`await`: it awaits the original inside `try`/`catch`, awaits a pause of `ms`, and then returns the value or throws the reason.)

## Approach

1. Map every `fn` of `functions` to a new function, keeping the order.
2. The new function returns a new promise and keeps its `resolve` and `reject`.
3. It calls `fn()` and attaches two handlers with `then`.
4. When the original resolves with `value`, wait `ms` with `setTimeout`, then `resolve(value)`.
5. When it rejects with `reason`, wait `ms`, then `reject(reason)`.

## Example 1, step by step

`functions` has one entry that resolves with 1 after 30 ms, and `ms = 50`.

- `delayAll` returns one wrapper. At 0 ms the judge calls it, which calls `functions[0]` and starts its 30 ms timer.
- At 30 ms the original promise resolves with 1, so the first handler starts a 50 ms timer.
- At 80 ms that timer fires and `resolve(1)` settles the wrapper's promise.

The answer is `[{ t: 80, status: "fulfilled", value: 1 }]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) to build the array of n wrappers; each call adds O(1) work and one timer.
- Space: O(n) for the wrappers.

## Pitfalls

- Returning promises instead of functions: `delayAll` must hand back functions, and the work starts only when one is called.
- Without a rejection handler, a failing original leaves the new promise waiting forever.
- Calling `resolve` in both handlers turns a failure into a success; pass a rejection on with `reject(reason)`.
- Waiting for the functions one after another makes the delays add up; each wrapper must wait only for its own original.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `functions`, `ms` | the original functions and the extra delay |
| `fn` | the original function one wrapper delays |
| `resolve`, `reject` | settle the wrapper's own promise |
| `value`, `reason` | the outcome of the original promise, passed on unchanged |

narration.1: delayAll receives the original functions and the extra delay ms.
narration.2: Build one wrapper per original function, in the same order.
narration.3: Calling a wrapper returns a new promise whose resolve and reject it controls.
narration.4: Call the original function and wait for its promise to settle.
narration.5: If it resolves, wait ms more and then resolve the new promise with the same value.
narration.6: If it rejects, wait ms more and then reject the new promise with the same reason.
